article_content: The global fashion industry is undergoing its most significant manufacturing rethink in decades. Once optimised almost exclusively for cost and scale, apparel supply chains are now being reshaped by geopolitics, climate risk, regulatory pressure, and persistent disruptions. The pandemic exposed the fragility of long, hyper-concentrated supply networks. Trade wars, tariffs, and regional conflicts have since reinforced a simple truth: efficiency without resilience is no longer viable. Against this backdrop, reindustrialisation (the strategic rebuilding of manufacturing capacity) has returned to the fashion agenda. Brands are diversifying away from overdependence on a handful of Asian hubs and reassessing where, how, and under what conditions clothing is made. In this global reset, Africa is re-entering the conversation. Long discussed as an ‘emerging sourcing frontier’ but rarely positioned as a true industrial contender, the continent is now attracting renewed interest from brands, investors, and policymakers. The question has shifted from ‘whether Africa can participate in global apparel manufacturing’ to ‘whether the continent can move up the value chain and emerge as a textile powerhouse in its own right.’ Why Reindustrialisation is Back on Fashion’s Agenda For decades, global fashion manufacturing followed a clear logic: lowest cost, maximum scale, minimal friction. That logic is breaking down. Rising labour costs in China and parts of Southeast Asia have eroded the wage advantage that once justified heavy concentration. Energy volatility, driven by geopolitical instability and climate stress, has added unpredictability to production costs. At the same time, compliance requirements around carbon, chemicals, and labour standards are tightening, particularly for brands selling into the EU and North America. Trade policy has also become a major force. Tariffs, export controls, and ‘friend-shoring’ strategies are pushing brands to diversify production geographically. Nearshoring and regionalisation are no longer niche strategies; they are increasingly seen as risk-management tools. Reindustrialisation, then, is not about reversing globalisation but rebalancing it. Brands are seeking manufacturing ecosystems that combine cost competitiveness with political stability, sustainability potential, and long-term scalability. Africa is increasingly being evaluated through this lens. Africa’s Structural Advantages in Textile and Apparel Manufacturing Africa enters this moment with several underlying advantages that are difficult to replicate elsewhere. First is demographics. Sub-Saharan Africa has the youngest population in the world, with millions entering the workforce each year. As aging populations constrain labour supply in Asia, Africa offers long-term workforce availability, critical for labour-intensive industries like apparel. Second is resource endowment. Africa produces approximately 10 per cent of the world’s cotton but exports the majority of it as raw fibre. The opportunity to retain value through local spinning, weaving, and garment production is substantial. Beyond cotton, the continent also has strong potential in man-made fibres, cellulosics, and bio-based materials. Third is geography. Africa’s proximity to Europe, the Middle East, and via Atlantic routes, the Americas enables shorter shipping times compared to Asia. In an era where speed-to-market matters, this geographic advantage is increasingly relevant. Finally, trade access plays a critical role. Regional integration through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), alongside Economic Partnership Agreements with the EU and other bilateral arrangements, is reshaping how African manufacturers access global markets and structure cross-border value chains. The State of Africa’s Textile and Apparel Industry Today Despite its potential, Africa’s textile and apparel sector remains unevenly developed. Countries such as Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Kenya, Ethiopia, Lesotho, and Mauritius have established export-oriented apparel industries, largely focused on cut-and-sew operations. Egypt stands out for its more integrated value chain, with strengths in cotton, spinning, and weaving. North African producers benefit from proximity to Europe, while several East African hubs initially built export momentum through preferential access to Western markets; an experience that provided early industrial learning but is now giving way to more competitiveness-driven sourcing models. However, across much of the continent, upstream textile capacity remains limited. Spinning, dyeing, finishing, and chemical processing are capital-intensive and energy-dependent; areas where infrastructure constraints persist. As a result, many African garment factories still rely on imported fabrics, limiting value capture and resilience. Industrial parks and special economic zones have helped bridge some gaps, offering shared infrastructure, tax incentives, and streamlined logistics. Yet scale remains modest compared to Asia’s deeply entrenched textile ecosystems. Trade Agreements and Policy Frameworks: Enablers or Constraints? The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) has played a formative role in the development of Africa’s apparel exports to the United States, particularly by enabling early manufacturing scale in East and Southern Africa. Although the programme formally expired in September 2025, a one-year extension through December 31, 2026 has provided short-term continuity for eligible exporters. However, the limited duration of this extension has reinforced a broader strategic reality: preference-based access can no longer be treated as a stable foundation for long-term industrial planning. With uncertainty surrounding renewal beyond 2026, brands and investors are increasingly cautious about anchoring sourcing and capacity decisions solely to AGOA. As a result, Africa’s next phase of apparel growth will be shaped less by trade preferences and more by competitiveness: productivity, cost discipline, sustainability performance, and the ability to serve diversified global markets. In this context, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) assumes heightened importance. By enabling regional value chains and reducing intra-African trade barriers, AfCFTA offers a more durable pathway for industrial development; one less exposed to external political cycles and better aligned with long-term manufacturing resilience. AfCFTA represents a longer-term structural opportunity. By reducing tariffs and harmonising rules across African markets, it has the potential to support regional textile value chains, where cotton grown in one country is spun, woven, dyed, and sewn across multiple neighbouring economies. National industrial policies also matter. Countries that align incentives, infrastructure investment, skills development, and trade strategy are better positioned to attract and retain manufacturing investment. Inconsistent policy signals, however, remain a risk in several markets. Foreign Investment: Who is Betting on Africa and why Foreign investment is emerging as one of the strongest signals that Africa’s textile and apparel sector is moving from speculative potential to strategic reality. Investors are no longer viewing Africa merely as a low-cost assembly destination; instead, they are positioning the continent as a long-term manufacturing hedge against geopolitical risk, rising Asian costs, and tightening sustainability regulations. 1. Chinese Investment: Cost Pressures and Market Diversification Chinese manufacturers remain among the most active investors in African textiles. Rising wages, energy constraints, and trade tensions, particularly with the United States, have accelerated outward investment from China into Africa. For many Chinese firms, Africa offers a dual advantage: competitive production costs and access to major consumer markets through a mix of temporary trade preferences, EU Economic Partnership Agreements, and increasingly diversified export routes. Crucially, Chinese investments increasingly focus on upstream and vertically integrated operations, including spinning, weaving, and fabric finishing. This reflects both technical expertise and long-term planning, as control over fabric production improves margins and supply security. Countries like Ethiopia, Egypt, and Tanzania have seen Chinese-backed textile parks designed to replicate integrated Asian manufacturing models, albeit at smaller scales. 2. Turkish Manufacturers: Speed, Proximity, and Vertical Integration Turkish textile and apparel firms are also deepening their footprint across North and East Africa. Unlike Chinese investors, Turkish companies are often driven by speed-to-market imperatives. Proximity to Europe allows manufacturers in Morocco, Egypt, and Tunisia to support fast-fashion and mid-market brands seeking shorter lead times and lower transport emissions. Türkiye’s long-standing expertise in vertically integrated textile production gives it a competitive edge in transferring skills, technology, and quality standards. Turkish investments frequently include dyeing and finishing facilities, critical stages that many African markets currently lack. 3. European, Middle Eastern, and Impact Investors European brands and manufacturers are increasingly supporting supplier investments indirectly, through long-term sourcing commitments, co-financing arrangements, or sustainability-linked loans. Middle Eastern investors, particularly from the Gulf, are drawn by Africa’s renewable energy potential and the opportunity to build lower-carbon textile hubs aligned with future regulatory requirements. Development finance institutions (DFIs) and impact investors are also playing a growing role, helping to de-risk early-stage projects through blended finance structures. Their involvement is particularly important for capital-intensive upstream facilities. Taken together, these investment flows suggest a shift from opportunistic sourcing towards ecosystem-building, where investors are betting on Africa’s ability to host integrated, competitive manufacturing clusters. Infrastructure, Energy, and Logistics: The Make-or-Break Factors If foreign investment is the catalyst, infrastructure is the foundation. Without reliable power, efficient logistics, and industrial-scale utilities, Africa’s reindustrialisation ambitions will remain constrained, regardless of labour or market access advantages. 1. Energy: Constraint Today, Opportunity Tomorrow Energy remains the single most critical bottleneck for textile manufacturing in Africa. Wet processing, spinning, dyeing, washing, finishing, requires consistent electricity, steam, and water. In many African countries, power outages, high tariffs, and reliance on diesel generators significantly increase operating costs and production risk. At the same time, Africa holds one of the world’s largest untapped renewable energy potentials, particularly in solar and wind. Countries such as Egypt, Morocco, Kenya, and Namibia are already investing heavily in renewables, creating opportunities for textile manufacturers to access cleaner, more stable energy sources. For brands facing carbon disclosure requirements and upcoming carbon border taxes, sourcing from renewable-powered factories is becoming a strategic advantage. The challenge lies in scaling energy infrastructure fast enough and aligning industrial development with national energy transition plans. 2. Logistics and Trade Facilitation Logistics inefficiencies continue to undermine competitiveness. Port congestion, inconsistent customs procedures, and fragmented transport networks add time and cost to exports. In fast-moving fashion markets, these delays can negate labour cost advantages. However, targeted investments are beginning to yield results. Port expansions, digital customs platforms, and trade corridors, such as those linking landlocked countries to coastal ports, are improving reliability in select regions. AfCFTA further strengthens the case for regional logistics integration, enabling intermediate goods to move more freely across borders. Industrial parks and special economic zones have helped mitigate infrastructure gaps by providing centralised utilities, transport access, and regulatory support. Yet their long-term success depends on connectivity to national and regional supply chains. 3. Water and Environmental Infrastructure Textile production is water-intensive, making access to clean water and wastewater treatment essential. Inadequate water infrastructure not only raises environmental risks but also limits the adoption of advanced processing technologies. Forward-looking investments in closed-loop water systems, effluent treatment plants, and water recycling are critical not only for environmental compliance but also for long-term operational resilience in water-stressed regions. Skills, Productivity, and the Workforce Challenge Africa’s demographic advantage is often cited as a strength, but labour availability alone does not translate into industrial competitiveness. The real challenge lies in productivity, skills depth, and workforce readiness. 1. From Labour Abundance to Industrial Capability Many African apparel factories operate at lower productivity levels than their Asian counterparts, reflecting gaps in training, production management, and technical specialisation. Skills shortages are particularly acute in areas such as textile engineering, machine maintenance, quality assurance, and compliance management. Building a competitive workforce requires sustained investment in vocational training, factory-level upskilling, and management development. Successful manufacturers often combine local hiring with international technical expertise during early stages, gradually localising leadership and operations. 2. Technology and Productivity Leapfrogging Africa has an opportunity to leapfrog older production models by adopting digital tools, automation, and data-driven manufacturing systems. Digital cutting, real-time production monitoring, and AI-supported planning can significantly improve efficiency if paired with appropriate skills development. Importantly, automation does not eliminate the need for labour; it changes the nature of work. Demand grows for technicians, engineers, and supervisors capable of operating advanced machinery. Aligning education systems with these emerging roles is essential. 3. Social Impact and Inclusion Apparel manufacturing has historically played a vital role in providing formal employment, especially for women. As Africa reindustrialises, ensuring decent work, fair wages, and safe conditions will be critical to sustaining social license and political support. Youth employment is another strategic dimension. With millions of young Africans entering the labour market each year, a well-structured textile industry could become a cornerstone of inclusive industrial growth if skills pathways are clearly defined. Sustainability as Africa’s Competitive Advantage As sustainability shifts from a voluntary commitment to a regulatory and commercial requirement, Africa holds a structural advantage that few regions can replicate quickly. Unlike older manufacturing hubs burdened with legacy infrastructure, Africa’s textile sector is still being built, creating a rare opportunity to embed sustainability by design, rather than retrofit it later. 1. Renewable Energy Potential Africa possesses some of the world’s highest solar and wind potential, which however remains significantly underutilised. For energy-intensive textile production, this creates a powerful value proposition: factories powered by renewables can offer lower long-term energy costs, reduced exposure to fossil fuel volatility, and substantially lower carbon footprints. As regulations like the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and Scope 3 emissions reporting take effect, brands will increasingly favour suppliers that can demonstrate low-carbon manufacturing. African factories powered by renewables could therefore gain preferential sourcing status as well as cost competitiveness. 2. Cleaner Industrial Footprints Many African industrial zones are being developed with modern effluent treatment plants, water recycling systems, and waste management protocols. This positions the region to leapfrog some of the environmental challenges faced by Asian hubs, where decades of unregulated growth have left deep ecological scars. 3. Alignment with ESG and Impact Capital Africa’s sustainability narrative resonates strongly with ESG-focused investors, development banks, and impact funds. Projects that combine job creation, climate resilience, and circular production models are increasingly able to access blended finance, lowering capital costs and de-risking expansion. In this context, sustainability is not a constraint on Africa’s industrial ambitions; it may well be the very lever that enables them. Can Africa Move Beyond Cut-and-Sew? One of the most critical questions shaping Africa’s textile future is whether the continent can move beyond basic garment assembly into higher-value manufacturing. 1. The Limitations of Cut-and-Sew Cut-and-sew operations are relatively easy to establish and labour-intensive, making them attractive entry points. However, they capture only a small fraction of the total value in the fashion supply chain. Overreliance on assembly exposes countries to razor-thin margins, buyer power imbalances, and rapid relocation risk. 2. The Case for Upstream and Midstream Integration True industrial transformation requires investment in spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing, finishing, and textile innovation. These stages generate higher margins, stronger supplier leverage, and more skilled employment. Countries like Egypt and Ethiopia are already demonstrating what is possible. Egypt’s long-standing cotton heritage, combined with new investments in spinning and finishing, positions it as one of Africa’s few near-fully integrated textile ecosystems. Ethiopia’s industrial parks, while still maturing, were explicitly designed to attract vertically integrated investors. 3. What it will Take Moving up the value chain requires: Without these enablers, Africa risks remaining locked into low-value segments even as global demand shifts towards higher-quality, traceable, and sustainable textiles. Risks and Structural Constraints Despite strong momentum, Africa’s reindustrialisation is far from guaranteed. Several structural risks could derail progress if left unaddressed. 1. Policy Inconsistency and Bureaucracy Frequent policy changes, inconsistent enforcement, and administrative complexity can deter long-term investors. Textile manufacturing requires predictable timelines and regulatory clarity, especially for capital-intensive upstream facilities. 2. Fragmentation Across Borders While AfCFTA promises regional integration, implementation remains uneven. Non-tariff barriers, customs delays, and incompatible standards continue to restrict cross-border supply chains, limiting Africa’s ability to function as a single manufacturing market. 3. Infrastructure Gaps Outside a handful of industrial corridors, many regions still lack the energy, logistics, and water systems required for advanced textile production. Without coordinated infrastructure planning, industrial growth risks becoming geographically uneven. 4. Global Competition Africa is entering a fiercely competitive landscape. Asian manufacturers are upgrading technologically, automating aggressively, and improving sustainability performance. Africa must compete not only on cost, but on reliability, quality, and compliance. The Road Ahead: What Would It Take to Succeed? Africa’s path to becoming a global textile powerhouse is achievable with coordinated action across stakeholders. Success will depend on whether Africa’s industrialisation is treated as a strategic project, rather than a cost-saving experiment. 1. For Governments 2. For Investors 3. For Brands 4. For the Workforce Africa stands at a critical juncture in the evolution of global fashion manufacturing. Rising costs, geopolitical uncertainty, sustainability mandates, and supply chain reconfiguration are reshaping where and how textiles are made. Few regions are as well-positioned, or as vulnerable, in this transition as Africa. The continent has the labour force, market access, sustainability potential, and growing investor interest to become a major textile and apparel hub. Yet without deliberate action to build integrated value chains, upgrade skills, and address structural constraints, these advantages could slip away. Reindustrialising fashion in Africa is a choice; one that requires commitment from governments, investors, brands, and development partners alike. If executed thoughtfully, Africa could emerge as the next textile powerhouse and a model for climate-aligned, inclusive industrial growth. If not, the opportunity may pass, leaving behind fragmented factories and unrealised promises. The question remains ‘is the global industry ready to invest, seriously and sustainably’, in making that future real. Reindustrialisation is being driven by supply chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions, rising labour costs in Asia, and stricter sustainability regulations. Brands are seeking more resilient, diversified manufacturing networks that balance cost, stability, and environmental compliance. Africa offers a young workforce, abundant cotton production, growing regional trade integration through AfCFTA, and proximity to major markets such as Europe and the Middle East. These factors create favourable conditions for long-term textile and apparel manufacturing. Key challenges include limited upstream textile capacity, unreliable energy supply, logistics inefficiencies, skills shortages, and inconsistent policy environments. Addressing these structural constraints is essential for building competitive textile ecosystems. Yes, but it requires investment in spinning, weaving, dyeing, and finishing facilities, along with technical education, stable infrastructure, and access to long-term capital. Integrated value chains allow countries to capture higher value in the fashion supply chain. Many African countries have strong renewable energy potential and are building modern industrial zones with cleaner infrastructure. By embedding sustainability from the start, African textile manufacturing could offer lower-carbon production aligned with global ESG and regulatory requirements. article_title: Why Seasonal Planning is Losing Relevance in Fashion
sub_title: Seasonal planning refers to designing and launching collections around Spring/Summer and Autumn/Winter cycles. It is losing relevance because long lead times, inaccurate demand forecasts, and rapidly changing consumer trends make rigid cycles inefficient and costly. Brands face issues such as unsold inventory, heavy discounting, and inflexible supply chains. The model forces early commitments, leaving little room to respond to real-time trends, often resulting in lower margins and missed demand
article_content: For decades, most apparel brands and retailers across the world have relied on a two-season cycle, Spring/Summer (SS) and Autumn/Winter (AW), under which brands design, manufacture, and launch collections aligned to specific seasons. The process begins nearly a year in advance, with design teams forecasting trends and studying runway shows in fashion capitals like Paris, Milan, and New York and fabric mill trade shows. These events involve significant costs, including travel, sourcing discussions, and vendor negotiations. Once trends are identified, designers create collections that move through sampling, sourcing, production planning, and bulk manufacturing. After six to nine months of preparation, the collections reach stores, where retailers coordinate synchronised launches, so the entire assortment arrives together to present a cohesive visual story to customers. What it Entails Because lead times can stretch up to nine months, brands must forecast demand across markets well in advance. However, forecasts often miss the mark, so brands have made peace with 50–60 per cent sell-through at full price, with the rest getting cleared through end of season discounts. Such markdowns erode margins and expose the risks of long-range forecasting. In 2018, H&M’s operating profit tumbled by 62 per cent while grappling with ~$4.3 billion of unsold inventory after overestimating demand for certain collections. The Operational Complexity Seasonal, forecast-based planning creates several inefficiencies that brands must constantly correct. First is the challenge of unsold inventory management at store level, which must be transferred between stores, discounted, or cleared through outlet channels or online. In 2022, Gap Inc.’s merchandise margin fell by five per cent, with more than half the decline attributable to higher discounting. Second, because the entire supply chain, from yarn manufacturers to fabric mills, follow the same calendar, factories and brand team face intense bursts of activity followed by periods of underutilisation, leading to capacity wastage and operational instability. Third, to ensure coordinated collection launches, production timelines are locked months in advance, elongating lead times, and leaving little room to respond to emerging trends. This rigidity also forces brands to adopt a ‘spray and pray’ approach: produce a wide variety of styles and hope that some will resonate with customers. Over time brands have faced disastrous consequences of this rigidity: ASOS missed a key demand window due to delayed inventory arrivals, while Under Armour was slow to respond to the shift from performance wear to casual streetwear. Long time-to-market was one key factor attributed in Forever 21’s bankruptcy as it failed to meet customers’ demand for constant newness. Why the Model Exists The two-season model originated in Western markets where sharp weather shifts made clothing strongly climate-driven. Indian brands continued this practice assuming that trends evolved slowly, and customers demand freshness every six months. The industry also assumed most fashion products shared similar lifecycles, i.e., about six months of spring-summer or autumn-winter. The Indian Fashion Cycle In tropical climates like India, only ~15 per cent of apparel assortments like heavy winterwear or peak summer garments, are truly weather-driven, and even these are relevant to barely six per cent of the country. The remaining 85 per cent, like T-shirts, shirts, dresses, and denim, sell year-round. Also, in India, festivals and marriage dates influence purchases more than climate. Yet the two-season model persists, creating commercial and operational challenges. Moreover, in the last few years social media has increased exposure to emerging trends and created a need to update wardrobes frequently. On the distribution side, online marketplaces have enabled brands to do multiple, even weekly drops of new styles with low inventory risk. As consumer behaviour evolves, the future lies in flexible assortment strategies aligned with customer demand rather than rigid seasonal calendars. While winter jackets, swimwear, or monsoon-specific clothing remain seasonal, most categories can shift to dynamic, trend-driven release cycles. Trends will differ: something like Oversized T-shirts will follow short trend cycles driven by youth culture and social media, requiring rapid design-to-store timelines while the wardrobe must-haves like denim, basic tees and formal wear will have longer lifecycles. Rethinking the Model Ultimately, brands must shorten the design-to-store lead time and align assortment strategies with customers’ buying pattern. Brands like Shein are adopting advanced systems to detect emerging trends faster through monitoring of online searches, social media sentiment. Brands like Zara and Boohoo reduce the development to store lead time through vertical integration by platforming fabrics, and owning the supply chain, accelerating time-to-market to as little as 15 days. Brands like Athleisure Basics, Stitch Fix etc facilitate low MOQs per style to facilitate smaller experimental production runs, while D2C brands are pioneering online-first product testing to validate demand digitally before physical store rollout. In the Indian market, Snitch launches new styles every 25 days, while Zudio conducts 52 micro-launches annually, aiming towards sustained inventory velocity and reduced obsolescence risk. The real lesson is not that one should adopt fast fashion nor stick to the two-season cycle. Brands should define how their product offering drives customer purchase behaviour—seasonality, trends, or core wardrobe needs, and align their organisational processes and supply chains accordingly. The decline of seasonal planning signals a broader shift in how fashion operates. Rigid calendars built on long forecasts are increasingly misaligned with real-time demand, especially in markets where climate plays a limited role. As consumer behaviour becomes more dynamic and digitally influenced, brands that prioritise speed, flexibility, and demand-driven decision-making will be better positioned to reduce risk and improve margins. The future lies not in abandoning structure entirely, but in adopting adaptive models that balance trend responsiveness with core product stability. Seasonal planning refers to designing and launching collections around Spring/Summer and Autumn/Winter cycles. It is losing relevance because long lead times, inaccurate demand forecasts, and rapidly changing consumer trends make rigid cycles inefficient and costly. Brands face issues such as unsold inventory, heavy discounting, and inflexible supply chains. The model forces early commitments, leaving little room to respond to real-time trends, often resulting in lower margins and missed demand opportunities. Consumers now expect frequent newness driven by social media and online platforms. Purchasing is influenced more by trends, occasions, and lifestyle rather than strict seasons, especially in markets like India where climate-driven demand is limited. Brands are shifting towards flexible, demand-driven models with shorter lead times, smaller production runs, and frequent product drops. article_title: Beyond Linear Sales: How Data is Building Fashion’s Second-Life Economy
sub_title: It refers to a system where garments are designed, tracked, and managed across multiple use phases, generating value beyond the first sale through reuse, repair, resale, and material recovery. DPPs assign a digital identity to each product, enabling traceability, lifecycle tracking, compliance reporting, and better decision-making across design, sourcing, and recovery stages. Data enables item-level visibility, helping brands assess durability, predict performance, ensure regulatory compliance,
article_content: For most of modern fashion history, the industry’s responsibility ended at the point of sale. Design, sourcing, production, and logistics were optimised to move products into the market quickly and cheaply, while what happened afterwards (in returns, reuse, disposal, and circulation) remained largely outside formal business models. That separation is no longer sustainable. In 2026, regulatory pressure, cost volatility, and material risk are forcing apparel companies to account for garments well beyond their first commercial use. What is emerging is a structural shift towards a second-life economy, one in which products are designed, tracked, and managed as long-term assets rather than single-transaction goods. This transition is being driven less by changing consumer preferences and more by hard operational realities: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) frameworks, Digital Product Passport (DPP) mandates, rising input costs, and the growing financial exposure of short product lifespans. As a result, fashion is moving away from linear sales logic and towards lifecycle-based systems that prioritise durability, recovery, and value retention. The central question facing the industry is no longer how to move more volume, but how to extract more value per product over time while maintaining compliance, resilience, and cost control. From Afterthought to Architecture: Formalising Product Circulation Historically, garment circulation beyond first use was unplanned and largely invisible. Products exited brand control once sold, entering fragmented downstream pathways that rarely fed information back into design, sourcing, or merchandising decisions. The emerging second-life economy reverses this logic. Circulation is now being engineered upstream. Design teams are beginning to consider longevity, repairability, and material recovery as core performance metrics rather than sustainability add-ons. Supply chains are being evaluated not only for speed and cost, but for how effectively products can be serviced, retrieved, and reintegrated over time. This shift is being accelerated by several converging forces: Together, these pressures are transforming product circulation from an informal externality into a designed system that requires measurement, governance, and optimisation. Data as the Backbone of the Second-Life Economy At the centre of this transformation is data. A second-life economy cannot function without item-level visibility, where individual garments are treated as traceable assets rather than anonymous units. Technologies such as DPPs, RFID, NFC, and QR-based identifiers assign persistent digital identities to products. Unlike traditional SKU-based tracking, these identifiers remain with garments across multiple use phases, locations, and condition states. This infrastructure enables three critical operational capabilities. In this context, data is the operating system connecting design, sourcing, logistics, and recovery. From Platforms to Distributed Ecosystems The early institutionalisation of extended garment use relied heavily on centralised platforms that aggregated supply and demand. While these platforms played an important role in legitimising non-linear product flows, their structural limitations are now becoming clear. Centralised models struggle with margin compression, inconsistent quality control, limited transparency, and weak integration with upstream design and sourcing decisions. By contrast, the second-life economy emerging in 2026 and beyond will be more ecosystem-based than platform-centric. Distributed ecosystems break down the value chain into interoperable functions, each handled by specialised actors. Instead of one dominant intermediary, value creation is spread across a network of partners that collectively manage product lifecycle performance. This architecture mirrors how other asset-intensive industries such as automotive leasing or industrial equipment servicing, manage long-lived products at scale. In practice, this means: This modular structure allows systems to scale without centralising operational risk or capital intensity. It also improves resilience: when one node underperforms, the system can adapt without collapsing. Critically, ecosystem models allow brands to retain ownership of lifecycle data, which is fast becoming one of the most valuable strategic assets in fashion. Rather than losing insight into product performance after first use, companies gain continuous feedback loops that inform design, sourcing, and pricing decisions. As DPP requirements advance in the EU and beyond, ecosystem-based approaches also offer a practical path to compliance, enabling brands to integrate multiple service providers without fragmenting accountability. New Value Creation Models Based on Time The most profound shift enabled by second-life systems is more economic than environmental. Fashion’s traditional growth logic monetised volume: more units sold, more seasons launched, more inventory pushed into the market. In a world of material scarcity, regulatory oversight, and demand volatility, this model is increasingly fragile. The second-life economy introduces a fundamentally different logic: value is created over time, not at the point of sale. Under this model, garments are treated as revenue-generating assets whose economic performance unfolds across multiple phases. This has several strategic implications. 1. Design Becomes an Investment Decision : Choices around fabric quality, construction, modularity, and repairability directly influence lifetime yield. Poor design decision reappears as accelerated depreciation, rather than just disappearing after clearance. 2. Pricing Models Evolve : Initial pricing increasingly reflects expected lifetime performance rather than just brand positioning or trend value. Products designed to endure, circulate, and recover effectively command structurally different economics. 3. Revenue Diversification Increases : Instead of relying solely on first-sale margins, brands can generate value through: 4. Risk Profiles Improve : By retaining visibility and partial control over products post-distribution, companies reduce exposure to demand shocks, inventory write-downs, and regulatory penalties. Importantly, these models do not eliminate production; they optimise it. Growth is decoupled from raw material throughput and increasingly tied to system efficiency, product intelligence, and operational coordination. Moving forward, competitive advantage will belong to companies that can quantify and manage lifetime value per product as well as margin per unit. Global Implications and Equity Considerations Extended garment use has always been global in practice, even if it was rarely acknowledged in strategy. For decades, garments circulated across borders through informal, opaque channels that shifted material burdens downstream without transferring decision-making power or economic participation. The emergence of a data-driven second-life economy creates an opportunity to rebalance this dynamic, but it does not guarantee it. Item-level traceability introduces visibility into flows that were previously invisible. In theory, this enables better forecasting, infrastructure planning, and shared value creation across regions. In practice, outcomes will depend on who controls the data and how it is governed. A more equitable second-life economy would recognise several realities: There is also a geopolitical dimension. As regions implement divergent regulatory frameworks, particularly around DPPs and waste responsibility, interoperability and mutual recognition will become critical. Countries that invest early in second-life infrastructure may gain strategic leverage in future trade and compliance negotiations. Conversely, without coordinated standards, the risk of fragmentation increases, creating parallel systems that benefit a narrow set of actors while excluding others. For brands operating globally, equity will become an ethical concern and a system stability issue. Uneven value distribution undermines long-term scalability and increases political and regulatory risk. Structural Risks in a Data- Driven Lifecycle Model While data-driven lifecycle management promises greater efficiency and accountability, it also introduces a new category of structural risk for fashion companies. As garments become traceable assets and lifecycle performance becomes measurable, weaknesses that were once obscured by volume-driven growth models are exposed. 1. Data concentration and dependency is one of the most significant risks. When lifecycle intelligence is controlled by a narrow set of technology providers or platforms, brands risk losing strategic autonomy over product performance insights. This can create vendor lock-in, limit interoperability, and weaken negotiating power as regulatory requirements intensify. 2. Governance complexity is another unresolved challenge. Item-level tracking crosses jurisdictions with differing data protection laws, trade rules, and consumer privacy standards. Without harmonised governance frameworks, brands may face fragmented compliance obligations that increase operational friction and legal exposure. 3. Algorithmic distortion poses another risk. Pricing, grading, and allocation models trained on incomplete or biased datasets may systematically undervalue certain geographies, materials, or use cases. Over time, these distortions can reinforce inequities and undermine trust in lifecycle systems. 4. Strategic vulnerability: From an organisational perspective, data transparency introduces strategic vulnerability. Design shortcuts, poor material choices, and weak supplier practices no longer disappear after first sale. Instead, they re-emerge as accelerated depreciation, elevated recovery costs, and measurable underperformance. For many organisations, this requires a cultural shift from short-term margin optimisation to long-term accountability. 5. Cybersecurity and data integrity risks cannot be overlooked. As garments become digitally identifiable assets, lifecycle databases themselves become high-value targets. Compromised data undermines not only compliance but also valuation, planning, and trust across the ecosystem. Managing these risks will require more than technology adoption. It will demand shared standards, cross-sector collaboration, and internal governance structures that treat lifecycle data as critical infrastructure rather than operational metadata. What Leadership will look Like Leadership in extended garment use will not be defined by symbolic initiatives or headline commitments only. It will be measured by system performance, integration, and resilience. Leading organisations will demonstrate several distinct capabilities: In short, leadership will be less visible in marketing narratives and more evident in operational metrics. The evolution beyond informal garment circulation marks a critical turning point for fashion. What was once framed primarily as a moral or environmental aspiration is becoming an operational discipline defined by infrastructure, data, and governance. This shift does not automatically deliver sustainability outcomes. What it does deliver is ‘measurability’. It makes performance visible, comparable, and accountable across products, regions, and organisations. In a data-driven second-life economy, circularity will shift from something brands claim to what they demonstrate. Longevity, recoverability, and lifecycle value move from abstract goals to tracked indicators that shape financial, regulatory, and reputational outcomes. This transition will be uncomfortable for many companies. It exposes inefficiencies, design failures, and misaligned incentives that were previously masked by growth. Yet it also offers a path to greater resilience in an industry facing material constraints, policy pressure, and volatile demand. Beyond 2026, the most competitive fashion organisations will be those that extract the most economic, material, and social values from each product they create. The second-life economy is thus no longer peripheral to fashion’s future. It is where credibility, competitiveness, and responsibility converge. It refers to a system where garments are designed, tracked, and managed across multiple use phases, generating value beyond the first sale through reuse, repair, resale, and material recovery. DPPs assign a digital identity to each product, enabling traceability, lifecycle tracking, compliance reporting, and better decision-making across design, sourcing, and recovery stages. Data enables item-level visibility, helping brands assess durability, predict performance, ensure regulatory compliance, and optimise value extraction over time. Unlike centralised platforms, ecosystems involve multiple specialised partners handling repair, logistics, and recovery, allowing scalability, resilience, and better integration with brand operations. Key risks include data dependency on tech providers, governance complexity, cybersecurity threats, algorithmic bias, and increased exposure of poor design or sourcing decisions. article_content: Epson’s digital textile printers are at the forefront of a move towards more efficient, sustainable textile printing. We all have that perfect pair of jeans, the fit, the colour, the style that feels made for us. But behind the seams lies a concerning reality: producing a single pair consumes nearly 3,781 litres of water 1 , enough to sustain one person’s drinking needs for approximately five years 2 or keep a shower running for more than seven hours 3 . In a country where 163 million people lack access to safe drinking water 4 , this is more than a statistic; it’s a serious point for reflection. India’s textile industry contributes 2.3% to GDP and employs over 45 million people 5 , yet it remains one of the largest consumers and polluters of water. Wet processing units, where fabrics are dyed, printed, and finished, are particularly resource-intensive. In hubs like Tirupur and Faridabad, groundwater depletion and contamination have reached serious levels. For the textile industry, this indicates a need for transformative technologies that can change production practices. Digital Textile Printing: Smarter, Cleaner, Faster Digital printing offers one of the viable solutions. Unlike traditional rotary or screen methods, it requires minimal pre- and post-treatment, especially with pigment inks that avoid extensive steaming and washing. Epson’s Monna Lisa ML-13000 digital textile printer can reduce water use by up to 97% 6 compared to conventional textile printing. Epson Monna Lisa ML-13000 Direct-to-Fabric Printer Beyond sustainability, digital printing also enables on-demand production, contributing to a reduction in overstocking and waste. Compact systems placed close to consumption centres shorten supply chains and deliver fashion in only the required quantities. “The future of fashion lies in responsible innovation,” says Samba Moorthy, President, Epson India. “Through our advanced digital printing technologies, Epson is enabling manufacturers to reimagine their production processes by reducing water use, cutting waste, and embedding sustainability at the heart of fashion manufacturing.” Beyond Printing: Closing the Loop Epson is also developing Dry Fiber Technology for textiles, currently in prototype. This technology defibrates used garments and mill waste into base fibres, which can be transformed into new non-woven fabrics. The defibering process is waterless 7 , addressing both water usage and the world’s low recycling rates for clothing. At Paris Haute Couture Week, designer Yuima Nakazato showcased garments in non-woven fabric made using Dry Fiber Technology. To do this, he used recycled clothing and production waste, demonstrating that high fashion can also incorporate sustainability. Designer Yuima Nakazato's collection at Paris Haute Couture Week / photography by Gio Staiano These innovations point to a future where style and responsibility go hand in hand. The next time someone slips into their favourite jeans, they should ask themselves: How were they made? Could they have been made differently? article_content: Summer is more than a season; it is a vibe, a feeling, and, of course, a wardrobe challenge. While the sun blazes outside, your mission is to stay effortlessly chic without compromising on comfort. And the secret weapon? Fabrics. The right textile does not just make you look stylish, but also determines how comfortable you feel, how long your garments last, and even how responsible your fashion choices are. From crisp linen shirts to silky Tencel dresses, summer fabrics have the power to transform your wardrobe. Choosing the right fabric is about more than fashion; it is about lifestyle. Natural fibres like cotton, linen, bamboo, and rayon dominate summer clothing for a reason. Cotton is lightweight, breathable, and moisture-absorbent, perfect for hot city days or seaside strolls. Linen, with its airy, textured weave, has long been a symbol of relaxed elegance, keeping you cool while adding a hint of sophistication to any outfit. Bamboo and rayon fabrics offer a silky feel with excellent breathability, making them ideal for flowy dresses, skirts, and tops that move with you. What’s Driving Summer Fabric Choices in Retail Recent retail insights show that cotton and linen together accounted for more than 45 per cent of summer apparel sales in 2025, highlighting their enduring popularity. Shoppers instinctively gravitate towards fabrics that are soft, lightweight, and easy to style. Tip for the discerning consumer: always feel your fabric before buying. Softness, lightness, and texture are your allies in the battle against summer heat. Understanding how fabrics perform in retail can also give you a leg up in curating a smart wardrobe. Linen shirts, cotton tees, and rayon dresses are perennial summer bestsellers. Their versatility of being adaptable from casual daytime wear to semi-formal evening events makes them retailer favourites. In Mumbai, for example, linen shirts saw a 30 per cent sales spike in April–May 2025 compared to synthetic alternatives. Cotton tees, especially in pastel or neutral shades, remain wardrobe staples. These trends are not just numbers; they reflect consumer instincts for comfort, style, and practicality. By paying attention to what sells, you can make informed choices that balance trendiness with longevity. The Rise of Sustainable Fabrics in Summer 2026 Summer 2026 also marks a significant shift towards sustainable fabrics. Organic cotton, bamboo, Tencel, and recycled materials are gaining traction, blending comfort with eco-consciousness. Consumer research indicates that 38 per cent 1 of summer shoppers now factor sustainability into their purchasing decisions. Taking note of this, retailers are introducing eco-friendly collections and labelling fabrics to highlight environmental benefits. For shoppers, this is an opportunity to combine style with responsibility: choose garments that feel luxurious, last longer, and contribute to a smaller environmental footprint. Sustainable fabrics are no longer niche; they are the new must-have for summer wardrobes. But even the most beautiful fabrics need proper care. Cotton and linen, if maintained correctly, can last multiple seasons, while cheaper synthetics may lose texture, shape, and comfort after a single summer. To protect your investment, hand-wash delicate fabrics, use mild detergents, avoid direct sun when drying, and rotate your wardrobe to minimise wear. Proper care ensures that summer staples stay soft, breathable, and stylish year after year, turning your wardrobe into a collection of reliable, chic essentials rather than disposable fast-fashion items. Fashion is more than just fabric; it is also about colour, texture, and visual appeal. This summer, pastel cotton shirts, earthy linen trousers, and flowy rayon dresses dominate consumer preferences. Retailers report that lightweight natural fabrics in bright, airy, or neutral shades outperform synthetics consistently. Top summer fabrics for 2026 include cotton, linen, rayon, bamboo, and Tencel—a combination that balances comfort, style, and sustainability. These textiles are not just practical; they are statement-makers, defining the aesthetics of summer style. Knowing which fabrics to invest in can also help you create a versatile summer capsule wardrobe. A breathable cotton shirt can be paired with linen trousers for a polished casual look. A flowy rayon dress works perfectly for brunch, beach days, or evening strolls. And with sustainable options like bamboo or Tencel, you can achieve elegance while supporting eco-conscious fashion. This is the era where style meets responsibility, and smart fabric choices are the bridge between the two. Ultimately, summer shopping is no longer just about chasing trends or picking the prettiest colours. It is about understanding how fabrics function, how they feel, and how they perform both for the wearer and the planet. From natural classics like cotton and linen to rising stars like bamboo and Tencel, each fabric has its unique story, benefits, and role in your wardrobe. By investing in fabrics that balance comfort, aesthetics, and sustainability, you are not just upgrading your wardrobe but elevating your summer lifestyle. Summer 2026 is about making choices that are informed, stylish, and responsible. Pay attention to your fabrics, care for them properly, and choose pieces that suit your daily life while reflecting your values. Whether it is pastel cotton tees, earthy linen trousers, or silky Tencel dresses, your wardrobe can be a testament to smart, chic, and sustainable fashion. Remember: style is not just what you wear; it is also how your clothes make you feel, how long they last, and the footprint they leave behind. article_content: In recent years, the intersection of fashion and women’s sports has evolved into a dynamic and influential domain, reshaping not only athletic performance but also cultural narratives around identity, empowerment, and visibility. Once confined to purely functional considerations, sportswear for women has transformed into a powerful medium of self-expression, innovation, and commercial significance. Today, fashion in women’s sports is not merely about aesthetics; it is a strategic blend of design, technology, inclusivity, and storytelling. The global women’s sportswear market was valued at $167.8 billion in 2025 1 . It is expected to grow steadily, reaching $178.3 billion in 2026 and approximately $265.4 billion by 2034, reflecting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.1 per cent over the forecast period. This growth is primarily supported by a rise in women’s participation in fitness and sports activities, along with increasing awareness of health and wellness. The expanding popularity of athleisure, which combines athletic wear with everyday fashion, is also contributing to market demand. Additionally, advancements in fabric technology and a stronger focus on sustainability by leading brands are playing a key role in driving market expansion. This evolution is also reflective of the growing global recognition of women athletes, whose visibility has elevated the importance of what they wear both on and off the field. As media coverage and brand investments in women’s sports continue to expand, fashion has emerged as a key interface between athletic performance and public perception. Consequently, sportswear now operates at the intersection of utility and influence, shaping trends that extend far beyond the sporting arena. The Evolution of Women’s Sportswear Historically, women’s athletic apparel was designed with modesty and restriction in mind rather than performance. Early female athletes often competed in cumbersome garments that limited movement and efficiency. Tennis players wore long skirts, while basketball players competed in bloomers: garments that restricted movement and reflected societal expectations of femininity. Over time, as women began to assert their presence in competitive sports, the need for functional attire became evident. The late 20th and early 21st centuries marked a turning point. Advances in textile technology introduced moisture-wicking fabrics, stretchable materials, and ergonomic designs tailored specifically to the female body. Brands began to recognise that women athletes required apparel that addressed both physiological and psychological needs, including comfort, mobility, and confidence. Performance-Driven Design Modern sports fashion is deeply rooted in performance optimisation. Apparel is now engineered to enhance athletic output through features such as compression technology, breathability, and temperature regulation. For instance, compression garments are designed to improve blood circulation and reduce muscle fatigue, while lightweight fabrics ensure agility and speed. A compelling real-life example is Serena Williams’s collaboration with Nike, where her tournament outfits, such as the compression catsuit worn at the French Open, were specifically designed to aid blood circulation and prevent medical complications, while also enhancing on-court performance. In sports like tennis and athletics, clothing is meticulously designed to minimise resistance and maximise movement. Consider the streamlined silhouettes worn by elite sprinters or the breathable skirts and tops seen on tennis courts: each element serves a functional purpose while maintaining visual appeal. Moreover, advancements in smart textiles are beginning to redefine the landscape. Wearable technology embedded within garments can monitor heart rate, body temperature, and movement patterns, offering athletes real-time data to optimise performance. Such innovations are increasingly being integrated into training regimens, enabling athletes and coaches to make data-driven decisions. As a result, sportswear is evolving from passive apparel into an active component of athletic performance and strategy. Fashion as Identity and Expression One of the most significant developments in women’s sports fashion is the emphasis on inclusivity. The industry is increasingly acknowledging the diverse needs of athletes across different body types, cultural backgrounds, and levels of ability. Adaptive sportswear, for instance, caters to athletes with disabilities by incorporating features such as easy closures and adjustable fits. Similarly, modest sportswear options have gained traction, enabling women from various cultural and religious backgrounds to participate in sports without compromising their values. Size inclusivity is another critical area of focus. Brands are expanding their size ranges and investing in research to ensure that performance is not compromised for athletes of different body types. This shift not only broadens participation but also fosters a sense of belonging and empowerment. Breaking Barriers Through Fashion Fashion has also played a major role in challenging gender norms and advocating for equality in sports. Uniform regulations, in particular, have been a site of contention and change. Female athletes have increasingly voiced their concerns about restrictive or impractical dress codes, leading to reforms in several sports. For example, in disciplines like gymnastics and beach handball, athletes have successfully campaigned for more flexible uniform options that prioritise comfort and personal choice. These changes highlight the importance of agency and respect in sports governance. Furthermore, fashion has become a platform for activism. Athletes use their visibility to address issues such as gender inequality, body positivity, and social justice. Apparel often serves as a medium for these messages, whether through symbolic colours, slogans, or design elements. The Influence of Athleisure The rise of athleisure has blurred the boundaries between sportswear and everyday fashion. What was once confined to gyms and playing fields is now a staple in urban wardrobes. This trend has been largely driven by women’s sports, where functionality and style coexist seamlessly. Athleisure reflects a broader lifestyle shift towards health, wellness, and comfort. Consumers increasingly seek clothing that supports active lifestyles without compromising on aesthetics. This demand has encouraged brands to innovate and diversify their offerings, further strengthening the connection between sports and fashion. Some noteworthy examples for this include : Sustainability in Sports Fashion As environmental concerns gain prominence, sustainability has become a key focus in sports fashion. Brands are exploring eco-friendly materials such as recycled polyester, organic cotton, and biodegradable fabrics. Additionally, efforts are being made to reduce waste through efficient production processes and circular design models. Women athletes have also emerged as advocates for sustainable practices, using their influence to promote responsible consumption. This alignment of performance, style, and sustainability represents the future of sports fashion. Increasingly, brands are adopting transparency in their supply chains, allowing consumers to make more informed and ethical purchasing decisions. Innovations such as biodegradable performance fabrics and closed-loop recycling systems are further redefining how sportswear is produced and consumed. As sustainability becomes a core expectation rather than a niche preference, it is set to reshape both industry standards and consumer behaviour. The Future of Fashion in Women’s Sports Looking ahead, the integration of technology, inclusivity, and sustainability will continue to shape the trajectory of sports fashion. Personalised apparel, driven by data and customisation, is likely to become more prevalent. Athletes may soon have access to garments tailored precisely to their biomechanics and preferences. Moreover, the cultural influence of women’s sports is expected to grow, further elevating the role of fashion as a medium of expression and empowerment. As boundaries continue to blur between sport, fashion, and lifestyle, women athletes will remain at the forefront of this transformation. In parallel, advancements in smart textiles and wearable innovation will enable clothing to actively respond to environmental conditions and athletic performance in real time. The industry is also likely to witness deeper collaborations between athletes, designers, and technologists, resulting in products that seamlessly integrate performance science with contemporary aesthetics. This convergence will not only redefine sportswear but also influence the broader global fashion ecosystem. Fashion in women’s sports has evolved from a secondary consideration to a central element of the athletic experience. It embodies a complex interplay of performance, identity, and innovation, reflecting broader societal shifts towards inclusivity and empowerment. As the industry continues to advance, it not only enhances athletic performance but also amplifies the voices and stories of women in sports, making it an indispensable part of the modern sporting landscape. From Serena Williams’ groundbreaking outfits to WNBA tunnel walks, athletes are redefining what it means to be both competitors and icons. Fashion empowers women athletes, amplifies their voices, and reshapes global perceptions of sport and style. As women’s sports continue to grow in visibility and influence, fashion will remain a vital part of the narrative, merging athletic excellence with cultural leadership. Rising participation in fitness, athleisure demand, and innovation in fabrics and design are key drivers. Advanced materials, compression, and smart textiles enhance comfort, mobility, and data-driven performance. It ensures accessibility across body types, cultures, and abilities, promoting wider participation. article_content: Lower carbon footprint*, faster supply, responsible feedstock Hyosung TNC, the largest manufacturer of spandex by market share, announces that production of its new regen™ BIO Spandex derived from sugarcane is underway, a major development that began in 2024 with the company’s $1 billion investment in a new bio BDO (Butanediol) plant in Vietnam close to its established spandex manufacturing facility. From Fossil Inputs to Bio-Based Innovation: Rethinking Spandex at the Source BDO is a chemical traditionally made from non-renewable resources used to make PTMG (Polytetramethylene ether glycol), the key raw material used in spandex. In partnership with Geno, a sustainable materials leader, Hyosung TNC can now produce bio BDO directly from sugarcane through a one step process that replaces fossil fuel consumption and reduces carbon emissions. “With this development, Hyosung TNC is the first to establish the world’s only vertically integrated production system from bio-based BDO to bio-based spandex ensuring reliable production and supply stability without compromising the fibre’s performance,” said Sora Yoo, Vice President Marketing, Hyosung TNC. The company’s bio BDO facility has an annual production capacity of up to 50,000 tons of bio-BDO, with the potential to scale up to 200,000 tons per year over time. For complete transparency, the sugarcane feedstock, sourced from Brazil, is verified under the VIVE Programme. Hyosung TNC will showcase is new regen™ BIO Spandex at the Global Fashion Summit in Copenhagen this May 5 -7 where it will be a principal sponsor. * Final data will be validated and updated based on a 3rd party LCA. For more information, visit https://www.hyosungtextile.com/en Hyosung TNC’s regen™ BIO Spandex marks a decisive step towards aligning performance textiles with measurable sustainability. By integrating bio-based raw materials, scalable production, and verified responsible sourcing, the company is not only reducing dependence on fossil inputs but also strengthening supply reliability. As brands increasingly prioritise low-impact materials, this innovation positions Hyosung TNC at the forefront of the next phase of fibre evolution, where performance, transparency, and environmental responsibility must advance together. regen™ BIO Spandex is produced using bio-based BDO derived from sugarcane instead of fossil fuels. This reduces carbon emissions and enables a more sustainable production process while maintaining the same performance characteristics as conventional spandex. The sugarcane feedstock used to produce bio BDO is sourced from Brazil and verified under the VIVE Programme, ensuring responsible cultivation, traceability, and compliance with environmental and social standards. Hyosung TNC’s vertically integrated system, from bio-based BDO to spandex, ensures consistent quality, supply stability, and greater control over sustainability across the entire value chain.

article_content: KARL MAYER is inaugurating a TEXTILE INNOVATION CENTER with a grand opening from April 21 to 24, 2026 in Obertshausen, Germany. Showroom at KARL MAYER (China) KARL MAYER sees textile innovations as potential growth drivers for its customers, as a motor for business development and as real game changers for the entire textile industry. Innovation does not happen by chance. It is the result of close exchange with customers and brands, textile expertise and competence in textile machine engineering. This is why KARL MAYER is opening its TEXTILE INNOVATION CENTER (TIC)—a place to be for the entire textile world. Its size, equipment and offerings are unique worldwide. With a floor space of 5,000 m², the TIC provides everything that makes development processes faster, more efficient and more successful. Inspiration and Fresh Ideas in the TIC Showroom and INSPIRATION HUB A spacious showroom with a curated presentation of textile materials and applications opens up space for new thinking and fresh ideas. The latest samples from KARL MAYER’s textile product development range are displayed here alongside concept textiles and applications with real market potential. Trend collections straight from market scouting highlight the latest looks from all over the world. Everything is clearly structured into tried-and-tested textile categories: Fashion & Apparel, Sports Textiles, Footwear, Home Textiles and Technical Textiles. In addition, there is an area for warp preparation applications. At the opening, TIC visitors will be able to discover innovative solutions for the growing workwear sector, including protective clothing for security and defence, outfits for beekeepers, clothing for medical professionals and stylish, comfortable items for the office. KARL MAYER is also opening its unique sample collection: the INSPIRATION HUB invites visitors to take a journey through almost nine decades of textile development. Customer Trials & New Developments on TEXTILE MACHINES The TIC supports customers, fibre manufacturers and, in particular, brands throughout their entire innovation process— from the initial idea to the near-series prototype. A range of innovative machines for WARP KNIT, WARP PREP and TECHNICAL TEXTILES is available to put ideas into practice. One of the highlights for WARP KNIT is a HKS 3-M EL PLUS, which redefines the application limits of the HKS family. The high-performance warp knitting machine impresses above all with its flexibility. The electronic guide bar control enables patterning without repeat limitations and with maximum efficiency. Thanks to the PLUS equipment—reinforced needles and knitting elements, more robust gang motion and sinker with extended movement—the range of products can be significantly expanded. A new feature is the ability to produce very open structures using coarse yarn counts for the manufacture of shoe fabrics or square marquisettes, each of which can also be implemented with coarse machine gauges. In the TECHNICAL TEXTILES sector, a modular fibre spreading set-up invites visitors to conduct processing tests and project work on new lightweight construction applications and solutions for the protection sector. Also, a warp knitting machine with weft insertion demonstrates its capabilities. It is particularly well suited for high-precision and gentle hollow fibre processing, thereby opening up new potential in the field of filtration. A high-performance machine for sectional warping of performance materials and a warp sampling machine for a wide range of applications are available for practical project work in the field of WARP PREP. Expertise, Networks and Genuine Spirit of Innovation, Thanks to TOP EXPERTS At the TIC, customers work side by side with KARL MAYER’s textile experts—and benefit from an extraordinary pool of experience, openness and innovativeness. As a team, the experts have decades of practical experience in a wide range of market segments—from Fashion & Apparel to Sports Textiles and highly specialised technical applications. They also contribute a strong international network of fibre manufacturers, technology partners, institutes and brands. Expertise for Professionals at the ACADEMY The KARL MAYER Academy, which is well established in the market, has become part of the TIC and continues to offer a unique training programme. The courses for customer technicians, brand employees, in-house service technicians and students stand for sound expertise, the very highest quality and a clear focus on the requirements of everyday production. Here, theory is not just taught but directly applied. KARL MAYER looks forward to presenting all these possibilities to customers, partners and the international trade press at the TEXTILE INNOVATION CENTER in Obertshausen during the opening event week. Save the date: April 21 to 24, 2026, Obertshausen – in parallel to Techtextil Frankfurt. For more information and registration to the opening event KARL MAYER’s Textile Innovation Center stands as a forward-looking platform where technology, expertise and collaboration converge to accelerate textile innovation. By bringing together advanced machinery, industry know-how and a strong network, the TIC enables faster, more efficient product development. It reinforces the company’s commitment to driving progress and shaping the future of the global textile industry. The TIC is a 5,000 m² innovation hub in Obertshausen, Germany, designed to support textile development from concept to near-series prototype. It combines advanced machinery, a showroom, and expert collaboration to accelerate innovation across textile segments. The centre features warp knitting, warp preparation and technical textile machines, along with a showroom, INSPIRATION HUB, and sample collections. It enables customer trials, product development, training through the KARL MAYER Academy, and collaborative projects with industry experts. The TIC is designed for textile manufacturers, fibre producers, brands, researchers and students. It supports innovation, testing, training and networking, helping stakeholders develop new products, improve processes and explore emerging textile applications.

article_title: Style Under Pressure: Shopping in a Soft-Dollar Economy

For consumers, this typically results in higher prices for imported fashion goods, reduced discounts, and more selective purchasing behaviour as overall affordability tightens. Luxury goods are often priced in euros, francs, or yen.
